processing: Ageing is storage, not a factory step: over years, slow oxidation and, in post-fermented teas, microbial activity change the leaf's chemistry. Teas commonly aged include sheng pu-erh, heicha, white tea (especially pressed), heavily roasted oolongs (re-roasted every few years) and some black teas. Green teas and light oolongs generally do not age; they go stale.
harvest_season: Any; what matters is the year of production and the years in storage, and both should be stated.
appearance_dry: Leaf darkens with age: a sheng cake goes from green-grey to brown and red-brown over a decade or two, white tea from silver-green to brown, roasted oolong from dark brown to near black.
appearance_liquor: Deepens from pale yellow to orange, amber and finally red-brown, staying clear in well-stored tea; a murky cup suggests damp storage.
appearance_wet: Supple brown to dark-brown leaf; wet-stored tea is darker, softer and smells of cellar.
taste_profile: Bitterness and astringency fade while honey, dried fruit, wood, camphor and medicinal or incense notes build; well-aged tea is smooth, sweet, deep and long rather than loud, and the storage climate (dry Kunming, humid Hong Kong or Malaysia) shapes the result as much as the years.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, a quick rinse (two for wet-stored tea), short steeps and many of them; aged tea rewards a thick clay pot and keeps giving long after a young tea has faded. Let a freshly unwrapped cake breathe for a few weeks after it arrives from storage.

vintage_note: This is the one category where the year is everything, and also where it is often faked. Sheng pu-erh is sold by production year, from young to decades old, with the factory, recipe number, wrapper and storage history all part of the price; any claim to very old tea needs provenance. White tea is sold by age under the saying 'one year tea, three years medicine, seven years treasure', which is marketing, not pharmacology. Aged oolongs are sold with the harvest year and the dates of re-roasting; aged heicha by batch year. Dry-stored, natural-stored and traditional (humid) storage should be declared.
description:
Ageing is what happens to certain teas when you leave them alone: over years in a cupboard, a warehouse or a Hong Kong basement, the bitter, green, aggressive compounds of a young leaf slowly transform into sweetness, depth and the woody, camphor-like, medicinal aromas that collectors pay for. It applies to raw and ripe pu-erh, other dark teas, white tea, heavily roasted oolongs and a few blacks; a green tea left for ten years is not aged, it is stale.

The changes are slow oxidation and, in post-fermented teas, the work of microbes, and they depend heavily on climate. The same cake stored dry in Kunming stays bright and slow; stored in humid Guangzhou, Hong Kong or Malaysia it darkens and softens faster and can pick up a cellar note. There is no single correct storage, only a declared one, and 'wet storage' pushed too far produces mould rather than age.

A well-aged tea tastes smooth, sweet and deep, with dried fruit, wood, honey and camphor and a cooling feeling in the throat, and it keeps going for many steeps. Brew it with boiling water, rinse it, and use short steeps in a clay pot; the usual mistake is to be timid with temperature. A cake fresh out of storage often needs a few weeks of air to shake off a flat, closed note.

Buying aged tea is buying a story, so the story needs evidence: the year, the factory or maker, the recipe or batch, the wrapper and the storage history. Fake 'antique' cakes with convincing old wrappers are a well-known fraud, so start with teas of modest age and clear provenance. Aged white tea cakes are often a cheaper way to taste what a decade does to a leaf.

Try a young and a ten-year-old sheng from the same region side by side, and then a dry-stored and a humid-stored cake of similar age: those two comparisons teach more than any description.

history:
Ageing as a recognised effect began by accident. Tea pressed into bricks spent long periods in transport and storage, exposed to the weather and to microflora, and green brick tea slowly oxidised and fermented into something new. That is one origin of the post-fermented teas.

Little is documented here about when people began keeping tea deliberately for its age, and practice varies by tea and region. Ripe pu-erh's controlled pile fermentation is a more recent production method.
